nameStory: Ampithoe valida gets its scientific name from Greek roots meaning 'around' and 'runner,' referring to how these small crustaceans scurry around marine environments. The species name 'valida' means 'strong' or 'robust' in Latin, likely describing this amphipod's sturdy build compared to its delicate relatives.
description: Ampithoe valida is a tiny marine crustacean called an amphipod that looks like a miniature sideways-swimming shrimp. These small creatures typically measure less than half an inch long and have flattened, curved bodies that give them their characteristic comma-like shape when viewed from the side. They're part of the diverse world of small marine invertebrates that most beachgoers never notice, but they play important roles in coastal ecosystems. **Note: Details about this specific species are uncertain due to limited reference material.**

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Laterally compressed (flattened side-to-side) body that curves like a tiny comma, with the back more arched than many other small marine crustaceans

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, typically under 12mm (half an inch) long, about the size of a fingernail clipping

idTips.label: Swimming style
idTips.description: Swims on its side in a distinctive jerky, darting motion rather than the forward swimming of small shrimp

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of long, thread-like antennae that are often longer than the body itself and wave constantly

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Seven pairs of legs with the front pairs modified into grasping claws for holding onto seaweed and debris

habitat: Found in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools and among seaweed beds where they can grasp onto algae and kelp. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are most commonly discovered clinging to eelgrass or rockweed in protected coves and harbors. **Habitat details are uncertain for this specific species.**

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, often found in shallow tide pools during low tide exploration.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to spot swimming among seaweed in warm tide pools and shallow waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper waters as coastal temperatures begin to drop.
seasonality.winter: Less visible and likely in deeper waters or protected microhabitats, rarely encountered by casual observers.

funFact: Amphipods like Ampithoe valida are sometimes called 'sea fleas' because they can jump impressive distances when disturbed - some species can leap up to 20 times their body length, which would be like a human jumping 120 feet!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small mysid shrimp or copepods in tide pools, but amphipods swim distinctively on their sides while mysid shrimp swim upright, and copepods have a more jerky, hopping swimming pattern without the sideways orientation.
contextualKnowledge: Amphipods are often overlooked but represent one of the most diverse groups of small marine crustaceans, with thousands of species worldwide. Many people mistake any small swimming crustacean for 'baby shrimp,' but amphipods are actually more closely related to terrestrial pill bugs than to true shrimp.
